speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce that the agricultural stabilization board has been authorized to support the price of sunflower seed to the producers of this crop in the provinces of Manitoba and Alberta at 4.15 cents per pound for Canada No. 1 grade, 10 per cent moisture, delivered at the crusher for the manufacture of sunflower seed oil. The support price is approximately 100 per cent of the base price.
The production of sunflower seed in Manitoba has been an important secondary cash crop in that province for a number of years and the board has supported the Manitoba producer price for the past two years. Production of sunflower seed in Alberta has been increasing in recent years, and it is now becoming an important secondary cash crop in that province. Alberta producers have therefore been included in this year's support program.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CURRENT SITUATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he is in a position to add anything to what he was good enough to tell the house yesterday on the serious situation in Laos.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CURRENT SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the 24 hours that have elapsed since I commented yesterday on the Laotian situation there have been certain positive developments. The military situation is that the Pathet Lao are continuing to make serious inroads into territory previously held by the royal Laotian government. The situation changes from hour to hour, and I think what appears in the press will give a general idea as to the situation in that regard.
A determined effort has been made by the governments of the United Kingdom and the United States to find a basis for peaceful negotiation with the objective of bringing an immediate end to the hostilities in Laos, of ensuring its neutrality and detaching it from the pressures of the cold war. There can be no doubt that this course is the one best calculated to serve the true interests of the Laotian people and prevent the present hostilities from spreading beyond the borders of that country, the result of which would be to create an even more serious threat to world peace.
As hon. members know, yesterday the United Kingdom laid specific proposals before the Soviet union. These call for an appeal from the United Kingdom and Soviet cochairmen for an immediate cease-fire in Laos, the first and the most necessary step; following that cease-fire, the reconvening in New Delhi of the international control commission for Laos, of which Canada is a member along with India and Poland.
Inquiries of the Ministry
When the commission so reconvened found that an effective cease-fire was in effect, an international conference would then be called. This conference could consist either of the countries represented at the Geneva meeting of 1954-that is, the United States, the United Kingdom, France, communist China, the U.S.S.R., Laos, Cambodia, South Viet Nam and North Viet Nam-or on the other hand, the larger conference along the lines proposed by Prince Sihanouk of Cambodia. This would extend membership of the conference to the members of the international supervisory commission for Laos and to Burma and Thailand.
The proposals which I have just outlined represent a sincere attempt to find common ground and would, if successful, accomplish the main objective of a neutral and independent Laos. There are, of course, grave difficulties still to be overcome, including the timing of a cease-fire in relation to the proposed conference and the identity of the government which would represent Laos at such a conference. The Canadian government fully shares the objectives of the United Kingdom proposal and, as I said yesterday, would be prepared to play its part in the international supervisory commission which would have an important function to perform in relation to the implementation of the proposals.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to hold up this resolution for any length of time. However, there is one matter which I think should be given some consideration before we go any further. I refer to the situation in which our old age pensioners find themselves in this country today. On July 19, last session, I had occasion to raise this matter, but unfortunately no decision was reached at that time. The matter was discussed until eleven o'clock that night but no decision was reached. The outcome was that the business of the house was arranged in such a way that we had no further opportunity to discuss this question during the following month of that session.
I am not going into all the detail that was discussed last year on this matter. However, I think in all fairness we should review the situation, particularly in view of the considerable support that government members gave it that day. I made a check and found that the matter was supported to a lesser or greater degree by the hon. members for

Chapleau, Parry Sound-Muskoka, Restigouche-Madawaska, York-Humber, Simcoe East, the present minister of northern affairs, the hon. members for Regina City, Prince, Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, Inverness-Richmond, Athabasca, St. James, Wetaskiwin, the present Minister of National Health and Welfare, and the hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet.
Some 15 hon. members on the government side, including two cabinet ministers, supported this proposal to a lesser or greater degree. However, I am sorry to say that all hon. members were not in support of the matter which was raised at that time, and the debate ranged from the full support that was given by the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska, who is unfortunately no longer with us, to lesser support by other hon. members. I do not know whether the fact that the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska is no longer with us has anything to do with the position he took on that occasion. I was talking to him some two weeks ago and he informed me that this was definitely one of the reasons that he moved from the house. He said it was because he felt the government had failed totally, completely and absolutely to carry out any of the promises they had made during the election campaigns of 1957 and 1958.
I should like to quote very briefly from the words of the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska as they are reported on page 6507 of Hansard for July 19, 1960. In the first column of that page, near the middle of the column, the hon. member is reported as having said:
I listened, as I said, very attentively to the representative of the C.C.F. group who introduced this amendment, as well as to the hon. member for Essex East. I could see nothing in what they said, with one possible exception, that was not in strict conformity with the solemn promises we officially made during the 1957 and 1958 elections.
Unfortunately some other hon. members did not agree completely with that and the debate ranged from a back-patting contest of saying how much the present government had done since they took over to an out and out condemnation of myself for raising this very embarrassing subject at that time.
I think it would be appropriate at this time to remind the committee once again, as I did last year, of just what is involved in this problem. I should like to quote from page 6521 of Hansard of July 19, 1960. I reminded the house of this matter last year, and I think this quotation is very appropriate. I am reported as having said:
I hope we have not lost sight of the problem with which we are faced by reason of all the diversions I have listed. It is not the Liberal party of 1923 or the Conservative party of 1931 that is going to have to deal with the problems facing old

age pensioners today. It is the members of the government and other members sitting in this house a few days before the end of the session who are going to have to decide if they are going to do anything for the old age pensioners other than utter kind words about them. We are going to have to make a decision before the end of the session so that the old age pensioners will know whether they are going to have to face another bleak winter before the government has another opportunity to do something for them.
That winter has come and gone and we do not seem any closer to solving this problem than we were when we debated it last on July 19 of last year. In spite of the kind words of many hon. members that day, and in spite of all the grand assurances of the 1957 and 1958 election campaigns, which were referred to by the former hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska, the cold facts of the matter are that this government have been in office for almost four years and they have failed to take this problem into consideration.
Something else has developed over that four-year period. It is something we hear very much about in this house from time to time. I refer to the problem of unemployment. I should like to refer to that problem only to relate it to the present problem of our old age pensioners. In this respect, as our communities across the country face increasing unemployment and as more and more of the unemployed come on to their relief rolls, we find that the municipalities are less and less able to give consideration to the relief of old age pensioners.
There is another factor which I think should be brought to the attention of the committee, and that is the increase in the number of old age pensioners over the last four years. If we look in the Canada Year Book we find on page 315 that old age pensioners between the ages of 65 and 70 have been increasing at the rate of 1.1 per cent every two years. This means that over a four-year period there has been an increase of between 300,000 and 400,000 in the number of old age pensioners who are in so many cases trying to live solely on the miserable pittance of $55 a month.
We also find that the cost of living has steadily crept up since the last increase in pension rates was given. The cost of living rose from an index of 121.9 in 1957 to 129.6 at the time the latest figures were given, a substantial increase for people who are trying to live on that sort of money.
There are two or three other things which I think should be listed to drive home the nature of this problem. The subindex shelter figure has risen from 134.9 to 144.6, and shelter is something which, obviously, no old age pensioner can do without. The cost of household operation has climbed-not as much as some of the other things, but it has climbed

Interim Supply
from 119.6 to 123.5. One of the most tragic things of all is the rapid increase in the cost of certain basic foodstuffs, and I should like to list two of the worst instances. Living on $55 a month, old age pensioners do not buy sirloin steaks; they have to look for the cheap cuts of meat. Yet we find that the index figure for the cost of stewing beef has risen from 52.6 to 140.5, an increase of 437 per cent, and the cost of hamburg from 37.9 to 123.7, an increase of 310 per cent.
Certainly this is something which the government must take into consideration and remedy. We find today that the prisoners in our federal penitentiaries, according to an answer given last year by the Minister of Justice to a question asked by the hon. member for Skeena, to be found on page 1386 of Hansard of February 23, 1960, cost $167.71 to maintain for a 31-day month. That is the difference, $167.71 for prisoners as against $55 for old age pensioners. If that is the free enterprise system the Prime Minister was talking about on television last week, it is a sorry picture. If it takes three times as much to maintain a prisoner in a penitentiary as the amount upon which we expect an old age pensioner to live, no wonder we have so many people in prisons under free enterprise systems. It is because they are treated better there than when they are outside.
Last year we heard so much about the amount of money involved in the resolution I moved. It was going to cost $200 million, and where was all that money to come from? Well, if the government have not got the answers to the problems which have to be met in our society, why do they offer themselves for the job? Where is the money coming from for the $1,250 million we spend every year on obsolete weapons? Where does the money come from for the $900 million interest a year it costs us to maintain our federal debt?
My point is that this government can do something when they want to do something, but it is very obvious, at least in connection with the difficulties of the old age pensioners, that they do not want to do anything. They shrug their shoulders and say "What can we do?" If they can do nothing it is time they got out and let somebody else try. Yet in the face of this problem we see the Prime Minister having the effrontery to go on television and pronounce pious platitudes about free enterprise versus socialism. It would be a joke if it were not such a tragedy.

It is not our intention to hold up interim supply, but there is one aspect of the vote which should give cause for alarm to all members of this committee and, for

that matter, to all Canadians. I refer to the extra public debt charges which are piling up at a very fast rate indeed.
At the end of the fiscal year about to start these extra charges since the present government came to power will amount to the staggering sum of $878.6 million, and most of this is for extra interest. This huge amount is arrived at by including the minister's estimate for these two years, that is for this fiscal year and the next fiscal year; and since the Minister of Finance has practically always been on the conservative side in his estimates as far as interest charges are concerned I have no reason to think that this staggering sum will be any less; in fact it is likely to be more.
So far we have not paid one cent of this extra interest nor are we likely to do so in the foreseeable future. The point is that we have borrowed this money, and this debt on account of these extra interest charges is snowballing at an alarming rate, particularly since it is being compounded every six months at a high rate. The hon. member from Carle-ton, the parliamentary secretary to the minister, tries to salve his conscience by talking about the per capita debt. All I can say is that Canadian babies are not being born fast enough to help spread the debt among them so as to give any weight to his argument.

The hon. member for Timmins has raised an extremely important subject matter and one which has, of course, been extremely important for many years, even in the years preceding the time the Liberal government was forced into establishing a system of pensions in 1925 and 1926; forced, I may say, because of the high principles of the socialists in the house at that time, under the late Mr. Woodsworth, a man for whom everyone in a position to judge had the highest regard, respect and admiration.
Even though the legislation in those days was totally inadequate from the point of view of the needs of our elderly citizens it was, nevertheless, a step along the road toward security for these people in their later years. It was primarily in 1925-26, in that period of time when there was a minority government, a matter of political consideration which the late Mr. King had in mind. This was one of the conditions on which he and his government could stay in office. The C.C.F. group in this chamber was then under the leadership of Mr. Woodsworth. We cherish the letter Mr. King wrote; in fact it is framed and hangs in Mr. Woodsworth's house.
The fact that nothing is said should not be taken as acquiescence, because these are not the facts.

The hon. member should pay more attention to what are facts. We all know

his ability to twist facts so they no longer appear factual. The hon. member's many years of experience in the Liberal party enable him to do this effectively. The fact is that Mr. King introduced amendments to the old age pension legislation because of political considerations in order to have support to remain in office and-I am sure my hon. friend will not disagree with this-it was the old guard Tories in the Senate who turned it down. Surely the hon. member will not deny that that is a fact.
That is the only part of the hon. member's statement with which I agree.

I am sure of that; none the less both statements are true and factual. It is an historic fact that political considerations have always been instrumental in the adjusting of old age pensions, fixing the amount and governing the regulations relating thereto. Political considerations relating to the 1949 federal election resulted in the establishment in 1950 of the joint committee on old age security. When the universal plan, as it is called, was instituted in 1951 and became effective in January 1952, it was primarily as a result of political considerations relating to the 1949 federal election.
The niggardly $6 increase introduced by the Liberal party coincided with the election of 1957. Again the old age pensioners were used as political footballs, but this time the technique backfired. The Conservatives with a different conscience from that which they displayed in 1925 and 1926 made promises in this regard, which incidentally have not been kept. When the Conservatives came into office old age pensions again became a political matter. A $9 increase was introduced in November of 1957 by the minority government, again coinciding with an election. The promises about pension increases have not been kept. Let me refer to a statement made at page 411 of Hansard of October 25, 1957. I quote from one on whom the hon. member for Essex East will look as an outstanding authority whose word could never be doubted. I propose to quote the hon. member for Essex East.

A very high
authority.

I am sure my hon. friend agrees with that statement. On that occasion the hon. gentleman quoted statements made by the present Prime Minister prior to the election. These are the words of the Prime Minister which the hon. member quoted:
We believe the old age pension is inadequate. We intend, this September, to call together a parliament and there and then fix a fair and reason-90205-6- 209i

able amount for the old age pensioners, indeed for the other pensioners, and also make provision for a formula whereby due alowance will be made in the future for the rising cost of living, providing that it continues.
The reference is to September of 1957. Of course the cost of living has continued to rise. Commenting on that statement the hon. member for Essex East said:
That last provision was an essential part of the program.
The present Minister of National Health and Welfare then interjected, "That will be looked after", and following another statement by the hon. member for Essex East an unidentified hon. member interjected "Give us time". The Minister of National Health and Welfare said this matter would be looked after, but we have waited three and one half years and nothing has happened. Perhaps he has not had time to look after it. Old age citizens deserve dignified treatment and should not be treated as political footballs, as they have always been treated by the old line party governments over the years.
In the short session of 1957 the Conservatives took a different approach and employed another election gimmick, as a result of which we got the Clark report. That report has been in the hands of the minister for some years and is probably languishing in a dusty drawer in his desk. In response to our persistent inquiries the minister says he still has it under consideration.
Study.

I venture to suggest the opinion that the minister, considering his great concern for political matters, will suddenly complete his study and come up with recommendations at a time that will coincide with the next general election, and again the old age pensioners will be used for political purposes. Our senior citizens have contributed greatly to the development and wealth of Canada over the years, and should not be treated in this shoddy manner.
A year ago I received some correspondence, as I am sure other hon. members did, from some senior citizens.

These words are just as true today as they were on December 18, 1959. Since that time I am sure all hon. members and the government have received similar briefs, lettters and references from elderly citizens who are humbly requesting that the government take into account their needs and their requirements and forget about the political aspect of the matter.
In the first place, it took the socialist point of view, against the tremendous opposition of the Conservative party and the Liberal party -except when they found it was politically expedient-to bring about old age pensions. It took the socialist philosophy in the first place to get this federal parliament and government into the field of old age pensions in the 1920's.
Ridiculous.
My hon. friend from Essex East says "ridiculous".
It is.

I would say to him with just as much force that he looks ridiculous in saying that factually true statements are ridiculous, even though he may want to prevent the country from knowing the truth about his party and how, like Moses, it also wandered for 40 years in the wilderness before it came up with a national health scheme. It was socialist philosophy that took into account the dignity that should be afforded to old people. It is regrettable to us that those-
Your philosophy is gone with the wind.

My friend says that our philosophy is gone with the wind. There are no more windy opponents of our philosophy in this house than the hon. member for Essex East and his colleagues. All they do is talk, talk, talk, and no action is taken unless it happens to be politically expedient to do so. This is one of the things that Mackenzie King was noted for over the years. He was noted for being able to move just enough at election time to get re-elected. The late Mackenzie King has a great follower in the present Prime Minister, who wants to emulate him at every turn. Political expediency is the order of the day rather than social justice. The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont agrees that the present Prime Minister is so like the late Mr. King that-
No.
Mr. Chairman, it is difficult enough to deal with the interjections and comments from the other side of the house without at the same time having to keep an eye on those behind me.
Try to be accurate.

My hon. friend says "Try to be accurate". In so far as my references to the Liberal party are concerned I have never been more accurate. We regret very much, Mr. Chairman, that people in their later years, who have contributed their talents, skills and ability to build up this nation and make it what it is today, should have to endure in some third floor cold-water flat a sort of meagre starvation existence from a small pension granted to them with great gusto only at election time and only when it will have some bearing on how the individuals may vote in that particular election. This has been the history of the Liberals and Tories; it makes no difference. I said, so far as the old age pensioners were concerned, the order of the day was political expediency and not social justice. With this the socialist element disagrees entirely.

We would welcome at any time, Mr. Chairman, the opportunity to deal with the Conservative party on the basis of socialist principles versus the so-called free enterpriser. The so-called free enterprisers, the merchant trading classes, were not in favour of old age pensions and are still not in favour of them. They have come to accept them in the same way the Liberal party and the Conservative party finally came to accept them, as a matter of social right and social justice.
The Minister of Finance is not with us today, but I am sure that his parliamentary secretary is equally capable in the field of administration in the Department of Finance as the minister, perhaps even more so. I am sure that if the hon. member for Carleton had the portfolio in his hands he would not make the bungling errors that the Minister of Finance has made. With the ability of the hon. member for Carleton, the parliamentary secretary, his knowledge of and intimacy with the intricacies of the Department of Finance, and the cabinet, he should be able to explain to the house what is government policy on old age pensions, whether the government are going to come along with an increase, and whether they do not think it is long overdue. Three and a half years is a long time for people to exist on a $9 increase, which was eaten up the next day by rent increases, increases in telephone rates and in the cost of living, and the like.
Does the hon member not think it is time this message was carried to the members of the cabinet, two of whom are with us today? Does the hon. member not think it is time they sort of probed the depths of their conscience and looked back upon the promises they made in 1957 with regard to the cost of living and brought them into account? Do not wait until the next election, and then be accused of playing political football with our elderly citizens. Does the hon. member not think our elderly citizens deserve a bit more justice and a bit fairer treatment than have been accorded to them since 1926?

Certainly this is too good an opportunity to miss. Unfortunately last year the C.C.F. were not able to get a vote on the motion of the hon. member for Skeena which would have forced the government to take a stand on this important matter of old age pensions.
I should like to refer to what I consider a disgusting situation. We are being asked to vote interim supply today. A great deal was said about our holding it up, and other things along that line, yet today we find the

minister does not even do parliament the courtesy of being here. He said there was a great rush to have interim supply voted, yet the minister is not in the house.

speechtext: I am sure the hon. member wants to be fair. He knows and the committee knows that the Minister of Finance is on a very important mission in Victoria today.

speechtext:
I did not know that. If the minister was going to be away he should have had the courtesy to say so last night when the request was made to bring this legislation forward today. I think the Minister of Finance is vitally involved in this matter of old age security. I think the time has come for us to give further consideration to the method of making old age security payments and the method of raising the money for such payments. In my opinion this is a responsibility of the Minister of Finance, in conjunction with those other ministers having responsibility for health and welfare in this country.
It has been generally agreed that there is a limit to the amount of payments to old age pensioners under the method we are following, and it is also generally agreed that there will have to be some change in the pension plan we now have with respect to the basis of making payments to our old age pensioners. This was recognized by the Prime Minister when he appointed Dr. Clark to investigate the whole matter of pensions not only in Canada, but also in the United States and other countries throughout the world where there are much better social security schemes that provide greater benefits to old age pensioners.
The former minister of national health and welfare had something to say about this matter, and it was not surprising to us that he took exception to the statement that it was not his party that was interested in old age pensions in the first place. Old age pensions were provided because pressure was brought to bear. I hope the same kind of pressure will be brought to bear after the next election and will force a complete change in social security programs for the Canadian people. As the hon. member for Timmins said, in
1958-59 we paid $5.41 per person per day to maintain prisoners in federal penitentiaries, while at the same time we were only paying our old age pensioners $1.80 a day. It seems to me something is wrong when we are paying more to keep people in penal institutions than we are paying our old age pensioners for the service they have rendered to our country during their years of employment. In addition, if an old age pensioner wants hospital or medical care he must either pay

Interim Supply
the premiums tor such care out of his old age pension or be declared an indigent after signing a form setting forth that he is not able to make the necessary payments. By a means test he is then able to get medical and hospital care.
As I have said, this is a very opportune time to speak about this matter. There will shortly be an election. Old age pensioners have always been under the impression that the only time they can get an increase in their pensions is when there is an election, particularly so when the situation does not appear to be too favourable so far as the government in power is concerned. As we are going to have an election shortly, I think it is time the present government stated what they intend to do for the old age pensioners.
An hon. member says that it is time for a change, which is quite true. I suggest to the Canadian people that if they are going to make a change they should make a real one and elect a party that will do something about such matters as old age pensions; not on the basis of a hand-out but on the basis of the changing environment of our country, our changing needs and the changing attitude of our nation.
The Prime Minister received a petition from the national old age pensioners federation which reads as follows:
The national old age pensioners federation presents for your attention the following resolutions and respectfully requests that prompt and decisive action be taken by the federal government.
Whereas the high cost of necessities makes a decent, healthy living on the present pension impossible- m which the government appears to be in agreement-as shown by the raising of the civil servants- pensions, grants, wages, etc., thereby acknowledging the necessity but omitting the above group of senior citizens who have helped to make these raises possible.
The argument has been put forward that the country cannot afford to increase the pension, that in doing so the incentive for economy and thrift would be destroyed-this is not necessarily so, for every dollar paid out to these pensioners would be spent on goods and services, thereby creating a decent standard of living for the consumer. This is sound democracy and business economics which the federal government acknowledged in principle when the family allowance was established without any contributory scheme or means test.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

With the wealth and rich resources of Canada these aged citizens should not have to be employed, as it

Therefore we respectfully request that immediate attention be given by the government to alleviate this chronic situation and that the following brief be given prompt consideration.

Mr. Chairman, at one o'clock I was dealing with some points made in connection with the pension matters raised by our hon. friends of the C.C.F. party, and I should like to say just a few more words on this subject. I do not intend to hold up this interim supply very long, but because this matter has been raised, and because of the terms in which it was raised, it is necessary for us to put ourselves on record in regard to such a vitally important matter as pensions.
The record of our party on this matter is not to be found so much in the words used in the House of Commons-though it may be found there, too-as in the legislation of this country over the last 25 years. That is more important than words.
I recognize that my hon. friend who preceded me attempted to point out-and this has been attempted many times-that the social security program which the Liberal party is proud to have carried out over the years had been forced on us. The answer to that rather ridiculous charge is to be found in the fact that this program was initiated long before there was a C.C.F. party in existence in this chamber. The hon. member for Timiskaming, of course, has attempted to disprove the record, and to throw some suspicion on our desire to continue this record and expand and enlarge it, by quoting from an hon. member of the Liberal party, namely Senator Crerar, who over the years has done a great deal for the party and for the country.
I have what I am sure the hon. member will consider to be an even more impressive authority to use against him in contradicting some of the things he said this morning because I could, if I so desired, use his own references to this matter last year when we were debating the principle of pensions and social security and when he said at that time, in contradiction to what he and his hon. friends have said this morning, that he was not wedded to any particular amount in regard to old age pensions and that he thought perhaps $75 a month at this time and in the present circumstances might be too high.
Those were the words used by the hon. member for Timiskaming when discussing this matter last year in this chamber, and if he reads Hansard of July 19, 1960 he will find a reference to that effect. I thought the hon. member at that time was adopting a very reasonable and responsible attitude reflecting a combination of economic reality and strong humanitarian considerations. It is that combination which characterizes the approach of the Liberal party to this question. We believe

and have always believed-and we have shown our belief in action-that humanitarian considerations are to be given first priority in the field of social security but that these must always be reconciled to fiscal and economic considerations as well.
Perhaps I may be permitted to quote from a distinguished authority in this field, namely myself when I spoke in a debate on this subject on July 19, 1960 as reported at page 6510 of Hansard of that year-
A natural modesty.

-and when I said, referring to the Liberal party:
We also recognize, while keeping in mind economic and fiscal considerations, that there are social considerations which are equally important, indeed more important, than fiscal considerations. We know that pension schemes and pension levels and social security programs generally can never be fixed but that they have to be adjusted and changes made as conditions in the country change.
That quotation indicates our position on this important matter. My hon. friends opposite in the Conservative party before and during elections have been lavish in promises in the field of social security and more specifically on the question of old age pensions. The Prime Minister is on record-and he has not as far as I know denied the record-as saying, and I quote from the statement he made on April 19, 1957, that "old age pensions should be high enough to meet needs".
That is an important and categorical statement. It would be very interesting if we had time-and I do not propose to take up the time of the committee to do it-to relate that categorical statement that pensions should be high enough to meet needs to what actually has been done by the government since it has had responsibility in the field of old age security.
In dealing with this point we think particularly of the Clark report. We think of the promises of the government to introduce with a minimum of delay a scheme of contributors pensions for old age security. We think particularly of the appointment after the election of a commission to look into this matter and we think of the Prime Minister's instructions to the first chairman of that commission to have his report ready in four months. The chairman of that commission, unable to do this kind of job within four months, resigned and so great was the haste in this matter he was succeeded at once by another chairman, Professor Clark, who did make a report on this very important question in March, 1959.

except to get periodically, after questioning by my friend the hon. member for Essex East, a reply from the minister concerned to the effect that he is still studying the matter. The hon. gentleman has been studying the recommendations of this report since March,

The position of the Liberal party on this matter has been made clear in this chamber on many occasions. It was made clear in the debate which took place on July 19, 1960. I do not think I can do better than put on the record the motion we moved at that time because it established our position then and it is our position today. This particular amendment to the motion to go into supply was repudiated, rejected and turned down by the majority in this house. Our amendment, which is found at page 6511 of Hansard, of 1960 reads as follows:
That in the opinion of this house the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing legislation to provide, in co-operation with the provinces, for increases in the old age pensions to meet special hardships endured by the recipients of old age security and old age assistance; to extend old age assistance to unmarried women and widows at 60 years of age; for the vesting of benefits in industrial pensions plans; and for a national contributory pension scheme, co-ordinated with existing provisions for retirement and old age security based on federal government contributions, as well as on contributions of employees, employers, and self-employed.
This is definite and concrete, Mr. Chairman. I think it is a very progressive program in this field. We have laid the program down in the House of Commons. It has been rejected in the House of Commons by the government, but it remains our position. I do not think I need detain the committee any longer, except to repeat that this program remains our position in this field.

We in the C.C.F.-New Party group have initiated this debate because we take the position that old age pensions are too low today and are a disgrace to the country; they should be increased. We have not had any reply from the government. We should like to have a reply as to their policy and what they intend to do about old age pensions because certainly it has beeen made crystal clear to the country that the Conservative party understands that old age pensions are too low but it has not yet decided to do anything about them. We would certainly be interested in learning of their stand.

We think that the problem, of old age pensions falls into two categories. First of all, there is need for an immediate increase in the pension that is now paid, one that will overcome some of the hardships that undoubtedly exist among old age pensioners in our country. Second, we believe a comprehensive social security system should be introduced to provide for retirement pensions based on the general average income and standard of living of Canadian people. We think that if such an old age security system were put into effect immediately it would have the advantage not only of providing much needed assistance to people on retirement but would do a great deal to stimulate the purchasing power of the Canadian nation. We suggest that such a plan is sound in every respect and that those people who are working today, those who are self-employed in small businesses and farmers should be permitted to pay into such a plan during the period of their income, and that at the retirement age they should receive a pension in keeping with the standard of living of other Canadians.
We believe that such a scheme should receive contributions from the ordinary citizen, the employee and the self-employed person. Contributions should be made by the employer-that is, by industry-and there should be contributions by the federal government. From contributions made to such a plan on a three-way basis would come the funds from which an adequate pension should be paid. I see no reason why such a plan could not pay to the beneficiaries concerned pensions of $100 to $200 a month. This would certainly not be high in relation to the average national income of the country. It should be sufficiently high so that the people who retire could look forward to a standard of living that was at least from 50 per cent to 75 per cent of the general income standards of working Canadians.
We think the time has come when further action should be taken in the social security field by providing increases in family allowances. After all, the family allowance legislation has been on the statute books since 1944. There has been a tremendous increase in the cost of living since that time. The index has risen from 75 to 126. To restore the purchasing power of the family allowance cheque, to say nothing about adding to its real value, would require an increase in the first category of payment of $6 a month to $10 a month, and in the category of $8 a month to $13 a month. Once the Canadian nation has decided that a given social security system shall be provided-in this instance, of family allowances it was decided back in 1944-parliament should not allow inflation to eat away and

tear down the value of such payments. I repeat, to restore the value of family allowances increases of this size would be required. I think that initially family allowance legislation was on a sound basis. Its purpose was to enable the parents of families to be better able to care for their needs, and this is the kind of program that is of benefit to the Canadian nation as a whole. This change, together with the old age security system that I have been speaking about, would provide a vast improvement in our present social security legislation.
There is a crying need for a system of portable pensions in Canada. After all, the present system or lack of system whereby certain pensions are provided by certain industries-and the pensions vary from industry to industry and are tied to an industry- means that a person in middle life is very reluctant to transfer his employment even if he is certain that at that time he would get a definite increase in income. He is reluctant because very often he loses his pension rights. To a certain degree we have tied or bound employees to industries which provide pensions. By allowing this system to grow up without an over-all social security plan we have contributed to the immobility of labour because, if persons should decide to make a transfer, they have to suffer a very severe loss in their pension rights. To overcome these difficulties we are suggesting now that there should be such an old age security system.

-we had produced a social welfare program which in its total dollar value represented a greater total percentage of the national budget than that of any other country in the western world save one. When hon. gentlemen talk about their protagonism for social welfare, let them not forget, as the Leader of the Opposition reminded us this morning, their hesitancy in the matter of family allowances. No one denies that Mr. J. S. Woodsworth was a great humanitarian. I sat with him in this house and knew him as well as any hon. member in the house. But that does not mean that because he had generous social views he is to be regarded, having sat in the opposition, as the author of any of these plans.
The fact is that when family allowances were first proposed in the industrial relations committee around 1926 Mr. Woodsworth was opposed to the concept. That is a matter of record. A political bribe, they called it.

By a former leader of the party and one-time premier of Ontario it was referred to as a political bribe. So when hon. gentlemen talk about their views on social welfare, and when members of the government consider the contributions they have made in that field, and notably when one takes into account the kind of speech made by the Prime Minister last Friday at

the Tory conclave, one can say that only by one's accomplishments can one appropriately be judged. In Canada it is the Liberal party which will lead the way in the field of responsible social reform in this country. The record is there to show this.
One can enter into competition as to what amount the pension should be. I think it is regrettable in our public life for any political party-men who have never held office but who look for the opportunity to do so-to promote a competitive race in the promotion of social benefits. I say that any political party that wants to be entrusted with the confidence of the Canadian people must demonstrate in its advocacy of particular social measures that it has a responsible appreciation of all that is involved. That is something that I regret I cannot say, has been done, having listened to the speech just made by the member for Assiniboia who aspires to be prime minister of this country.
As the Leader of the Opposition pointed out today, the fact is, that the Liberal party, having this record in the field of social welfare, recognizes that, with the existence and emergence of new problems in our industrial society, modifications have to be made, and increases have to be provided for in social benefits and in the field of old age pensions, family allowances and disability pensions; that new schemes have to be embarked on to meet new situations as they arise, and that these can be met possibly in the light of the nation's capacity to meet those obligations. One should not forget that all of these measures have to be provided for out of one source only; and that source, of course, is the hard work of the Canadian people. With that consideration in mind the Liberal party has put forward, as the Leader of the Opposition has reminded us, the program of the 1958 convention which continues to represent our position. The leader of the C.C.F. party failed to note what the Leader of the Opposition has said in that regard.
First of all, as to a further step in the implementation of health insurance against the hazards which can be provided for by medical care insurance, we do not believe that we should deal with this matter by way of a royal commission. Indeed, if we were going to do this by way of a royal commission we would not have taken three months to announce the personnel of it. The government announced the royal commission in the middle of November. All we have had from the Prime Minister or the government is the designation of a chairman, and no further progress has been made. One is left in doubt as to when this royal commission is going to be finally selected and when it is going to begin its operations.

We also believe in extending unemployment insurance because of illness. We believe in the expansion of pensions for disabled persons to include the partially disabled. As the Leader of the Opposition pointed out, we believe in the extension of old age assistance to unmarried women and widows 60 years of age. We believe in the improvement of family allowances with special reference to family allowances to students until they have attained the age of 18 years. We believe in the introduction of new pension plans with provisions for early vesting of benefits so that if an employee changes his employment he will retain the advantage of pension contributions previously made by him and his employer, so that in effect the pension follows the man. The leader of the C.C.F. party is by no means the spokesman for the only group that believes in portable pensions. Because the provinces have jurisdiction in this matter, I would call my hon. friend's attention to the lead of the Ontario Liberal party with regard to portable pensions.
Finally, as the Leader of the Opposition pointed out, we believe in the immediate consideration of a national contributory pension scheme co-ordinated with the existing provisions for retirement of old age security, the pensions to begin at age 65 and based upon the federal government contributions as well as contributions of employees, employers and the self-employed.
I doubt very much if the hon. member for Assiniboia appreciated fully what he was talking about when he referred to a contributory plan. He first of all confused it with a means test. He gave one the impression that he had that uncertainty of touch in this field that he sometimes alleges I have in another one. I can only say this with regard to this scheme. Having in mind the fact that we now have a universal system, and having in mind the fact that the federal government of the day in 1951 embarked upon the only universal old age security system to be found anywhere, we believe the time now has arrived when, in the light of experience and practice in the United States, we might well give consideration to supplementing our existing universal system with a scheme of contributory pensions that will provide for amounts relating to the contribution that will far exceed anything like the present basic amount of the old age pension. I think it is important that we should understand what this scheme is. It is because the hon. member for Assiniboia obviously does not understand that I feel I should like to say something about this today.

First of all, as the Leader of the Opposition reminded us, the government did promise the Canadian people in 1958 that we were going to have a scheme of old age pensions based upon a full contributory principle, along the lines generally known to apply in the United States. The fact is that since the election the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who does not take part in this debate, has had in his control the recommendations and the assessment of this problem by Professor Clark, but the government refuses to give the house any indication of what its intentions are. The minister said only ten days ago, in answer to a question of mine, that he was continuing to study the Clark report. I called his attention to the fact that last June he told me that he had completed his study, but that the government had not yet decided upon a course of action based on that study and the recommendations which he would, at some stage, make to his colleagues. In the absence of action there can be no justification for the government of the day having authorized the expenditure of money that went into producing this report, and there can be no justification for the Minister of National Health and Welfare, or for the Prime Minister not telling this house what the government policy is with regard to the adoption in Canada of a system similar to the old age survivors security system in the United States. Last Friday the Prime Minister promised that at the appropriate moment something would be done about pensions. What is the appropriate moment? Is the Prime Minister waiting until the eve of an election before announcing this? Is he hoping once again, notwithstanding the admitted need that now exists, to take advantage, during the course of an election, of a proposal in this field in order to enhance his own political position and that of his party? If that is the course being taken by the Prime Minister, I say that it is not a proper course, because if there was need in 1958 that need certainly exists today.
I should like to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who is not here today, what decision the government has arrived at and what decision the Minister of National Health and Welfare has arrived at. Is the minister now satisfied that the suggestion in the Clark report, that this would be too costly a scheme for Canada, really represents the government's policy? That is not the position this party takes.
It is to be noted that the proposal put forward and referred to today by the Leader of the Opposition is one that goes further than the old age security contributory system in the United States. That system in the United States is based exclusively on contributions from employee and employer. No

government contribution whatsoever is made under that system in the United States. However, because of our regard for the existing need we have included in our proposal contributions from the federal government also.
This problem of providing assistance for our senior citizens is one of the great problems facing us. Almost one million people in Canada, out of our 18 million people, are 70 years of age and over. Almost one million people are now in receipt of old age security universal pensions. Some 300,000 people between the ages of 65 and 70 are receiving old age assistance. Our population is ageing, and what is now a great problem in terms of numbers will continue to be a challenging problem. There is great need in the case of many of our people. This is one of the problems of this industrial age in which we live. We can meet it out of the present universal system by adding to the present cost of something like $600 million almost twice that amount in less than a decade.
Because of this consideration I think we must recognize the inevitability of superimposing on the existing old age universal system something that is in principle not unlike the system in the United States. I suggest that the government has been remiss in waiting all this time to take the house into its confidence with regard to its view on what should be done about the facts elicited in the Clark report. The government is certainly treating parliament with great disrespect and it is treating the people of Canada with very little respect when it causes a report to be prepared during the course of an election and keeps it under cover for two and a half years, giving no indication whatsoever as to what it proposes to do with it except to hint at political rallies what it might do as the time approaches for holding an election.
I think that for the Prime Minister and this government to play with the old people of our country in this way indicates the real concern the government has for their plight, particularly when we bear in mind what the Prime Minister said on February 12, 1958. This is what the present Prime Minister said, as reported in the Globe and Mail of February 13, 1958:
-Mr. Diefenbaker took his social security program one significant step further. Until now he has promised only a study of the U.S. social security system.
Tonight, he pledged: "We will bring about in Canada a rounded and effective contributory social security plan over and above-and I emphasize this-that which already exists".
Such a plan would provide Canadians with social security payments in addition to the $55 now paid under the old age pension plan.
Referring to the report his government has ordered, he said he had asked that it be made

The minister was quoted as saying that the kind of consideration being given to this question would involve the application of a system based upon eligibility, which in turn would be based upon need. That is nothing more than a means test. It should not be forgotten that in 1951 parliament decided to bring in a universal old age security system without a means test. It is interesting to note that the recommendation for that policy was made by a parliamentary committee whose chairman at that time was the present premier of the province of Quebec, Mr. Jean Lesage.
Parliament and the government accepted this report. I think it would be very difficult for the government to embark upon a new system that ran contrary to the attempt to eliminate a means test in the application of old age pensions in this country. If the government feels it cannot provide an extension to the existing universal system, then the provinces and the federal government ought to give consideration to the fact that something must be done immediately to meet the kind of case which was presented to the government by the mayor of Toronto. That could be done by the federal government in the interim along with the provinces. But over the long term, and as a basic program, I think we must recognize that it is desirable to adopt in this country the features of the old age survivor system in the United States, based, as it is, on a system of contributions from pensioners and employers with added contributions from the state.
If contributions from the state are not provided we shall encounter the same experience as that which was encountered in the United States when the scheme was first established there. It took 18 years before any real benefits were paid at all under the old age security system as conceived in the United States some 22 years ago. If we are to provide a system which gives immediate benefit to the people who will have made contributions, the only way in which that

could be done would be by adopting the course we pursue in the case of unemployment insurance where one third of the contribution is paid by the state.
In this industrial age there is no other course open to us than to provide these social welfare measures. Some call this welfare capitalism; some call this the welfare state; some call it a negation of the system of free enterprise. I prefer to recognize what has happened in the last half century. I prefer to recognize that our society has changed. It has changed gradually, and I hope it will continue to change gradually and under responsible direction. But our system cannot be maintained unless we recognize that in our effort to provide the maximum amount of private initiative, we must take provision at the same time for those classes in our community who do not have the necessary means in order to qualify for the assistance now made available in one form or another.
When we look at our heavy roll of unemployed today we might well ask ourselves: where would we be but for some of the social measures we brought in? Where would we be but for unemployment insurance? Well do I remember the criticism made of the Liberal government when it introduced unemployment insurance in 1941 and the suggestion that we were embarking on a form of state paternalism which would cause this country to become bankrupt. The same kind of criticism was levelled against Mr. Mackenzie King in 1925 when he introduced a system of old age pensions, only to have it turned down by a majority in the Senate which happened in that year to be made up for the most part of supporters of the Conservative party. The situation was the same when family allowances were introduced. It was said in criticism that we had become socialists, and that we had destroyed the private enterprise system. Let me say this to the Prime Minister and his colleagues on the benches opposite. The issue in the next election will not be the kind of issue he envisages. It will be the incompetence of this government and its failure to carry out its promises compared with the record which the Liberal government, when it was entrusted with office, was able to build up for the Canadian people and which included the provision of family allowances as well as these other social measures. Family allowances now provide almost three million families representing nearly 6,500,000 children every month with assistance in filling the gap between what a parent earns and what is needed to maintain these dependent children properly.
I have been aroused into making this speech by the suggestions of the hon. member for Assiniboia who holds himself up as the

only one who is interested in these matters, though the fact is that the Liberal party has led the way. The man who sits on my left is the leader of the party which has been first in the field of social welfare in Canada and the only party in this house which can legitimately criticize this government for having failed to carry out promises which greatly assisted it in being placed where it now sits, Mr. Chairman, to your right, but it will be for only a short time.

Fence sitters. He and his colleagues want to keep out of any controversy. A six-dollar party is what they were in 1957 and they are still a six-dollar party. speechtext: Order.
