speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sorry, but the rules say that there may be only one speaker at a time. The hon. member for Timmins has the floor.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I must confess that I fail to see how an attack on a provincial government in the federal parliament is going to be of any assistance with respect to the plight in which old age pensioners find themselves today. Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, in view of the comparison of the number of government speakers this year with the number last year, which was in the ratio of 15 to one, we can only be led to believe that the purpose last year was not to improve the lot of the old age pensioners but rather to avoid a vote. I do not know what other conclusion we can come to. Why have hon. members opposite lost interest in the period from July 19 last to now?
It may be that the idea of increasing old age pensions is too repugnant to the Prime Minister with his views on free enterprise. If the old age pension is too socialistic, then I suggest that the Prime Minister, or some other member of the cabinet or at least some member of his party should stand up in the house and tell us what the free enterprise solution is to the problem of our old age pensioners.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the resolution carries I should like to refer to something that was said by the Leader of the Opposition about what I had said. I am sure the Leader of the Opposition can afford to be fair and I am not quite sure that he was fair last year when dealing with this subject. At that time he was depending entirely on his

memory of something that had been said earlier in the debate. However, having had an opportunity to look at the record, he said today almost the same thing as he said then.
I pointed out at that time that old age pensions do not appear to me to lend themselves to great expansion as long as we neglect to bring in the large number of compulsory and voluntary pension plans found in the industrial sector of our economy. Therefore, it seems to me there is very little difference of opinion between the hon. member for Essex East and myself in this respect. He has indicated now that the Liberal party is pledged to put into effect an old age survivor assistance plan similar to that in the United States. He also implied that if we adopted a social security scheme such as that in the United States we would be able to implement the same benefits and thus place our elderly citizens in a much better position. I referred to bringing together industrial pension plans and the national old age security plan in order to provide a much better old age retirement fund than we now have. As found on page 6495 of Hansard for July 19 last I said:
We should pay our old age pensioners a reasonable amount based on the cost of living and the standard of living to which we are accustomed. It is not sufficient to provide old age pensioners with a roof over their heads and a subsistence diet consisting of bread, milk, butter and a small amount of meat. In arriving at a figure we should take into consideration the gross national product and the ability of Canadians to contribute to a plan that will enable our senior citizens to retire on decent standards. The time has come to consider this.
In my dealings with employees in various industries throughout the years I have never encountered any reluctance on their part to contribute to retirement funds, whether it be the old age pension scheme or a pension plan between the employee and employer. In every case, however, I found a great resentment on the part of the employee concerning those conditions that made it necessary for him to remain in the same job in the same plant under the same employer for a period of 25 years or more before receiving any benefit from the pension plan. These plans should be national in scope. People who retire should be granted a basic pension of $75 a month, and it would be advantageous for the Canadian economy and in the best interests of the security of our people if they could have a supplementary retirement pension equal to half the maximum salary they earned during their lifetime. Where the government contributed to the pension plan the $75 would be part of the retirement fund.
I went on to say this, and this is the part to which the Leader of the Opposition has referred:
I do not ask the government to adopt $75 as a fixed figure. It could be increased to this amount today, but within a month or six months if the Canadian dollar continued to decline it might be that $75 would be too much and the economy could not bear it. On the other hand, the rising cost of
Interim Supply
food, rent, clothing and medical care has made it imperative that the old age pensioner now receive $75.
Then I went on to recommend a study being made of the Clark report. What I was referring to there was the fact that at that time the Canadian dollar was dropping very rapidly and, having regard to the state of the economy generally, that it appeared to me that old age pensions should have some relationship to some standard or formula and not remain at a set figure. In the depths of a depression when the prices of goods fall markedly I can see that $75 a month might be regarded as a very large amount. However, I certainly stated that in terms of present conditions $75 a month was the minimum requirement and that it was likely that this figure would rise rather than fall. I suggested that the payments should be tied in with some formula, such as the gross national product or the cost of living as established by the bureau of statistics or some other formula which would provide flexibility and keep payments to old age pensioners in line with their needs.
There is nothing very difficult about understanding this matter. If our standard of living dropped very rapidly it might be that the Canadian economy could not afford to pay to old age pensioners any amount that would be out of line with the standard of living at such a time. On the other hand, under present circumstances I think we can now afford to pay old age pensioners more than $55 a month when the standard of living in the city of Toronto, for example, is such that the municipality must pay almost as much as the federal government to maintain a bare minimum standard for these people.
I do not understand why governments are reluctant to put into effect a national pension plan that would be based upon contributions by employees, employers and the government. I do not see any difficulty in establishing a pension plan such as that in Germany which will provide the worker with a pension half as large as his income in his highest five-year earning period. My hon. friend points out that the insurance companies will not allow it. I believe this is the reason why government annuity and superannuation provisions have not been developed to the extent of providing a national portable pension plan.
I would draw to the attention of the committee to the Department of National Revenue information bulletin No. 14 on pension plans for the purpose of the Income Tax Act. The Minister of Finance in his argument said that the reason that proposal had not been accepted or was no longer in effect was the

Interim Supply
same as that for which the so-called blue book had not been left in effect. He said that it was his opinion that vesting rights of pension plans must remain within the jurisdiction of provincial governments. I read his remarks at that time but I can see no reason why the Canadian government could not deal with vesting rights as it did with unemployment insurance. It will be remembered that it was considered that the responsibility for unemployment insurance was not within the jurisdiction of the federal government, but a change was made in the British North America Act allowing unemployment insurance to be implemented. With that fact in mind I would suggest that it would not be difficult to overcome the present problem. I suggest that the blue book sets out the principles and regulations regarding the method by which the pension plan should be introduced and operated.
I have had many inquiries from union members regarding this problem of vesting rights, and would bring to your attention that Mr. McCann suggested, in 1950 when he introduced this statement, how this matter should be treated. I should like to read the sections which those union members are interested in. Appearing at page 14 of the blue book under the heading "Part 10. Vesting" appears the following section:
(a)	The rights of the employees to the benefits provided under the plan must be stated. An employee must have an immediate vested right in contributions made by him.
(b)	The rights provided by employer contributions must vest in the employee within a determinable period, and particularly on the attainment by the employee of an age which would prejudice him in the event of severance from employment. Therefore vesting should be absolute upon attaining age 50, subject to a minimum period not exceeding 20 years of service or participation. There must be an absolute vesting upon attaining optional retirement age, subject to a reasonable period of service or participation.
(c)	Vesting of the employer benefits may be conditional upon the employee leaving in the plan his own contributions, or may be graduated by a stated percentage over a period of years. Vesting of the employer's contributions in the event of death prior to retirement is optional.
(d)	The terms of the plan may not subject the rights of employees under the plan to any claims by the employer or any other person. In particular, the funds available for employee benefits may not be held or used as security against any debt or defalcation.
(e)	If the number of employees covered under a plan is five or less, there must be an immediate vesting of all payments.
Many pension plans are being implemented across the country in many different categories, some not advantageous to the majority of employees in the plan. One plan was brought to my attention where the employer made all the contributions and therefore felt that until the employee, after long continuous

service with the company had reached retirement he had no vesting rights whatsoever. Other plans exist of course where the employee and the employer make contributions, but in those cases the employee, after a period of time, is given vesting rights in his contribution, but in most cases the employee is never given vesting rights until he has reached a specific age in regard to the contributions made by the employer. In many cases, the employee continues to feel, that the contributions made by himself and his employer is his own money because if these contributions were not made toward a pension plan he would be receiving the amount of money in the form of wages.
What does the term "vesting right" mean? It is my understanding that this term is interpreted to mean that after a three-year period of contribution to an insurance policy the subscriber has limited rights and at that time may in conjunction with his insurance company have a paid-up policy or may transfer the amount of his contribution to another type of insurance policy. It means he has certain rights in the funding of his pension plan and the right to take part in the decision as to whether it should be fully funded.
At page six of this Co-operative Commonwealth Federation letter to its council members, the following appears:
In discussing the subject of a national pension fund, the question immediately arises as to whether or not it should be fully funded. While this aspect of the subject will be discussed thoroughly at a later date, there are one or two observations that should be made here.
It is not at all necessary to place national superannuation on a fully funded basis. (The term "fully funded" means that if contributions ceased to be paid into a fund, there would still be enough money in the fund to pay up all benefit claims against it. Such a fund would have no deficit on capital account, or actuarial deficiency.)
In the case of private insurance schemes, there may be a good argument for maintaining the scheme on a fully funded basis, or avoiding a deficit on capital account. By nature a private company cannot be assumed to be a perpetual concern. A private company must also depend on its own, and therefore, limited resources. On the other hand, a compulsory national pension scheme is based upon a permanent body of contributors with unlimited life. There is no need to make provision against possible liquidation.
What would be required, however, is the assurance that the position of the national fund on current account be at all times sound.
This would mean ensuring that for a number of years ahead income was at least equivalent to expenditures by adjusting contributions whenever necessary. However, for a considerable number of years after the commencement of superannuation this problem would not exist. During this period income from contributions would greatly exceed benefits paid out.
While the primary importance of a national superannuation scheme is to provide adequate financial security in old age, it has also a national economic advantage. The accumulation of contributions under such a scheme would provide a substantial source

of investment funds for carrying out large-scale capital developments in Canada. This would be especially true for the first 20 to 25 years when contributions exceeded benefits paid out.
This matter of vesting rights is very important. It has been stated many times that only the Canadian government can carry out the full vesting of these pension plans. Many of the mines in the area from which I come cannot establish this type of pension plan because it would be impossible for them to put away the amount of money which would guarantee this pension to their employees. They could not do it on the basis of a portable plan; they could only do it on a limited scale pension plan where they have vesting for their employees only after ten years of employment.
This means that if a fund were established and the mine were closed down before the ten years had elapsed, those employees would not of course have been employed in the mine for the requisite number of years and would not have reached retirement age. There would be no way in which they could obtain this money after they had reached retirement age, because the company would be liquidated and would no longer exist. The Department of National Revenue could not guarantee that the contributions which had been made on behalf of these people would be available. The department would not be in a position to guarantee that the private company would have the money put away for this purpose. The money could easily be disposed of in the liquidation of the company.
For this reason it is very important that this matter of vesting be given very careful and immediate consideration. I suggest that when the former minister of national revenue, Mr. McCann, introduced this measure he was of the opinion that it would solve the problem that was self-evident in many of the plans his department was asked to approve.
A good, progressive move.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Yes; I am sure it was a good, progressive move. I can inform the hon. member who has interrupted that the unions are still interested in this matter of vesting.
They will get it when we again have a Liberal government.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
They cannot get it from a Liberal government; it was a Liberal government that withdrew this plan. This book is not to be found in the public library; it is not available to unions or anyone because that minister, Mr. McCann, had to withdraw it because it was impossible to put it into effect. The Minister of National Revenue
Interim Supply
knows this. He tried it again in 1959. He did not make it quite as clear then, because he did not specify vesting rights in as simple a form. However, he also had to withdraw it for exactly the same reason. This has been withdrawn and disposed of because neither the Liberals nor the Conservatives have yet found a way of dealing with this matter. The only way to do so is by putting into effect a national pension plan. A national pension plan is twofold in this respect. We will have to give the old age pensioner $75 a month, but we will have to look for methods of increasing this pension beyond $75 a month other than those which are being used at the present time.
We have mentioned several amendments that would allow us to meet a pension of $75 a month, but we have not solved the problem of establishing this plan. The Minister of Finance has said he cannot allow this vesting section in the Department of National Revenue's direction for the simple reason it contravenes what he considers to be provincial rights. The Minister of Finance says this matter comes within the jurisdiction of the provincial governments in connection with civil rights and liberties. There is no greater civil right or liberty than the matter of the old age pensioner being able to live out his last days enjoying those liberties and rights which should have been established for him during his many years of employment.
I think all that is involved here is a small amendment to the British North America Act. It may be that a former minister of the crown, now the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate, may be in a position later to do something about this matter. I do not know.
Hear, hear.
Never.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am not sure whether he will be in a position to do it. I hope this party will be in a position to do this.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I hope that what the hon. member has said is an indication that his party agrees to put into effect a national pension plan which will provide-
It is in the Liberal program now.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
That does not mean anything. I have not heard the hon. member endorsing the resolutions which came from his party's convention. I have never seen a group of people so reluctant to talk about those proposals as are the hon. members of that political party. I understand that the only person who really sympathized with them was

Interim Supply
the leader of the party. I do not know why he did this, because I have not yet assessed his reason for supporting most of these things.
If what the Leader of the Opposition has said is true, it means he is pledged to support these resolutions. However, I am pleased to know that even from his seat the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate says he will change this section of the British North America Act in order to make it possible for this program to be effected.
He will change it by a private member's bill.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I hope they will do what was done with regard to the Unemployment Insurance Act, which was a very forward step. I hope we shall no longer do what the Conservative government has done, namely hide behind the skirts of the provincial governments of this country. I hope the federal government will give leadership in this matter of social security, even if it means amending the British North America Act.
When this measure was introduced in 1950 it became self-evident very soon afterwards that this step should be taken in order to make the program possible. The minister did not see fit to do this. He did not even see fit to come to parliament and explain why he did not do it. There has been a great deal of reluctance on the part of our governments to say why they are afraid to give consideration to a national pension plan on a contributory basis in order to supplement old age pensions.
The only minister who has given us any clue as to the reasons for this reluctance is the Minister of Finance. He gave an explanation, but only after one of the government members said, "We cannot increase old age pensions now. If we increase old age pensions to $75 a month it will give us a $200 million deficit. We cannot increase them because we already have a deficit".
This is what provoked the Minister of Finance to get into the argument. There may be another reason. I do not know everything; I have difficulty in learning what little I do know. However, if the Minister of Finance, the Minister of National Revenue or their assistants say that what I have said is wrong, and they have found a way of doing this other than the way I have outlined, I hope the necessary steps will be taken, and I will support them to the limit.
I have worked in the industry of gold mining for 15 years. The gold mining industry has never had a lifetime of more than about 20 years. It is an industry in which very few people would ever be able to obtain a pension because they either do not live in

the industry long enough or the industry itself does not live long enough. We shall have to adopt a national pension scheme which will allow them to take the benefit of their contributions from one industry to another, and we shall need to supplement the payments made in order that they may be able to retire with reasonable comfort in their old age.
I am sympathetic toward part of the argument used by one of the Liberal spokesmen when he said we should give consideration to allowing the people themselves to help build a national pension scheme. However, employees in those sections of industry where there are no pension plans today have no alternative but to end their days under the old age security program. The only people who benefit are those in industries where unions are strong enough to force implementation of pension plans to which both employers and employees contribute. I do not think we should leave the situation as it is. I think we want to offer the opportunity to all Canadians to make contributions to pension plans and to help them to establish schemes which will return them at least half of their average wage in their best five years in order that they may be able to retire with respect, maintain the homes which they have taken a lifetime to buy, continue to run their cars and retain their position in society which they have been accustomed to hold.

I have no desire to prolong this debate beyond the length of time it has already taken. However, in view of the fact that I suspect there may be an inordinate demand for Hansard of today's issue for distribution throughout the country, I think I should say one word about all this discussion, reminding the committee at the same time that this is only a motion to grant interim supply.
We have today discussed the Bank of Canada, the textile industry, unemployment, fiscal matters and monetary matters. We have discussed a national pension scheme, the old age pension scheme and, now, the vesting of pensions as well as half a dozen other subjects which no doubt have not occurred to me. In fact, the committee has skimmed very lightly over every subject in this category, running as fast as Eliza did in "Uncle Tom's Cabin" when she ran across the ice of the river, and probably just as frightened.
It has been a beautiful display of theatre, and the friendly arguments between the two groups on the other side of the house, as to which should eliminate the other before it is itself eliminated, were no doubt greatly appreciated by government supporters and others.

Once again I stress that this is a motion for the granting of interim supply. There will be other debates. There will be a budget debate. The estimates of practically all the departments with the exception of the department of immigration have yet to come before the committee, so there will be many opportunities for these matters to be discussed at length. I would suggest also, with respect, that these motions are not usually regarded as providing an occasion for a policy discussion. Certainly it has not been the practice of any government, as I recall it, to make announcements of policy during a debate such as this one.
If we became involved in a discussion of all the matters raised today the debate would probably need to be carried on for another two or three days. As I say, we shall have further opportunities to discuss these matters later. The committee has spent a reasonable length of time at least-and I think that is a conservative statement-in discussing these questions up to now; and if hon. members feel that they have had ample opportunity for raising these problems I hope they will agree to get on with this resolution and dispose of this matter before five o'clock when we shall be considering private members' bills. As hon. members know, it is necessary to dispose of this matter and others in the immediate future. Without desiring to limit debate in any way, I hope this objective can be achieved. I promise hon. members opposite who have raised the questions and sought answers from the government that at the right time those answers will be forthcoming. We are not proposing at this stage of debate to satisfy the wishes of the opposition in all those respects because, as I mentioned, this is a stage of debate which heretofore has gone through within a few minutes and has been regarded as merely a technical matter.
Since the debate has gone on for this length of time, I suggest that with the consent and approval of all members we might get on with the practical steps necessary to implement this measure before five o'clock.

Before the item carries,
I wonder whether the minister is prepared to give an unqualified assurance that there will be another budget. That is a serious question.

We are disappointed that the Minister of National Revenue, the Acting Minister of Finance, should not have taken this opportunity to put forward the position of the government with regard to this very important question of an immediate increase in old age pensions.
Ways and Means
It is true that before 1956 it was not customary in dealing with interim supply to have a debate on questions of government policy. However, I think the practice has grown up since 1956 of making use of this stage of debate to put forward some of the proposals that may be in the minds of members. We regret very much that not a single member on the government side of the house has risen during this debate to speak in support of an increase in old age pensions though it is certainly clear to anyone who reads today's Hansard-and the minister referred to this matter-that it is very much in order during this discussion to talk about increases in old age pensions.
I should just like to make one further comment. It seems indicated that interim supply will be passed today. I was not certain at all that this would be the case. However, I think the government has arranged-I do not say deliberately; perhaps it is just one of those things which happen by coincidence-that the most controversial and, very often, the most vitriolic member of the house and of the cabinet, should not be in his place today to pilot this resolution through the house. There is no doubt in my mind that though this matter has taken a considerable time to deal with, the hon. gentleman's absence has expedited the discussion.

subsubtopic: DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, a great deal of discussion has taken place on these estimates and I shall attempt to avoid

repeating anything that has been said. The minister at an earlier date dealt with the various changes in his department. I do not intend to deal with those changes except to say I think they are good ones. I refer to the bringing of the wheat board and the board of grain commissioners under the Department of Agriculture. 1 think this action will result in better co-ordinated farm policy and will bring about a greater coordination in aid to farmers.
The endeavour to stress farm sales and find new markets is a commendable one. Perhaps to some extent it is directly as a result of the changes to which I referred, particularly the placing of the wheat board under the Department of Agriculture. Perhaps the board more fully realizes that the income of farmers depends on the board.
We all realize that the famine in China had something to do with sales of wheat in that country but similar circumstances were not evident in relation to sales to Czechoslovakia or Russia. I hope the Department of Agriculture will make every effort to regain and hold sales in our regular markets and that every effort will be made to make customers aware that our products are available to underdeveloped countries under the Colombo plan and through United Nations organizations.
Much has been said in this debate about farm income and cash income. In a way that would be clear to anyone who would take the time to study his figures the minister pointed out that cash income to farmers is moving in the right direction. I noticed recently that in the year 1960 the cash income was up 12 per cent. We are all glad to see this result.
The hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska quoted some figures that he said were from D.B.S. sources. Where he got them I am sure I do not know. I have some figures on my desk but they certainly do not correspond with those of the hon. member. He quoted prices at which products were sold, and said that they had decreased, but he did not refer to his own province at all. The index for that province is considerably higher than the index of prices in western Canada. He condemned to some extent the acreage payments to the western farmers. If he had referred to the index from which he quoted he would have seen that products sold on the prairies at prices considerably lower than those in eastern Canada, and particularly in his own province.
The hon. member for Beauce quoted from an article in Maclean's magazine, written by Peter C. Newman. He more or less pounced on the idea that the Minister of Agriculture
Supply-Agriculture
would never take the place of Johnny Apple-seed. He did not quote from the same article a paragraph that caught my eye. This paragraph is from the same article in Maclean's:
The Tories have ladled out nearly half a billion dollars to Canadian farmers since they took office. Their various programs and subsidies will this year amount to nearly four times as much as the farmers received during the last year of the Liberal administration.
He did not feel that this was worth putting on the record, but I do. The article goes on to refer to the great hope of the new Minister of Agriculture and suggests that he may take the place of Johnny Appleseed. Certainly, he is doing a tremendous job in selling agricultural products and in selling agriculture to Canada as a whole.
I do not intend to say too much about the C.C.F. party. Last night we heard a great deal about their aspirations, and perhaps today as well. For a long time the hon. member for Assiniboia has talked about what he would do for the farmers of western Canada. In considering how serious he and members of his party are, and how serious the official opposition are one must come back to the record in order to see whether it bears out their remarks. We have often reviewed what the Liberal government did during the 1940's, up until 1948. They would not lift the embargo on Canadian cattle going into the United States, much to the chagrin of the farmers in western Canada. They entered into an agreement with Great Britain which cost the Canadian farmer a great deal of money.
In looking back over the past record I notice that the socialists and the C.C.F. party supported this agreement and said that it was a good thing and that we should enter into it. Several members in the house at that time raised doubts and inquired whether some precautions should be taken in the consideration of this agreement. One of those members was the present Prime Minister and another was the then leader of the opposition, Mr. John Bracken. They both raised doubts with regard to this agreement, as to whether it was a good one and whether every consideration was taken in connection with the years ahead. One must realize that over the years the C.C.F. party has tried to climb onto anything that would bring them votes. This was evident in the farmers' march on Ottawa not so long ago. Another instance was the demand for deficiency payments. They raised this issue and blew it up as high as they could. They are now going to do the same thing with the feed mill question, blowing up out of all proportion the situation that actually exists.
I hold in my hand a clipping from the Kinistino Post dated Wednesday, May 27, 1959. The headline reads:

Supply-Agriculture
Minty Loptson declares:
C.C.F. sabotage of wheat board has cost farmers millions.
The article goes on to say that Mr. Loptson charged that the minister of municipal affairs for Saskatchewan made a speech in which he said that in 1951 the British people had already paid the Canadian producer $182 million more than they needed to pay on the contract for wheat delivered. The article goes on to say that Mr. Attlee was made aware of this view and, of course, when more money was asked for by the then government it was refused. Certainly no money was given. I do not like to quote this article. I am sorry that the hon. member for Assini-boia is not in the house, but I went to the trouble to look up the debates in the Saskatchewan legislature in order to see whether the Saskatchewan member had actually said that we had already received $182 million more than we should have received for our wheat. At the bottom of page 3 of the proceedings of the legislative assembly of Saskatchewan for February 14, 1951, I find that Mr. McIntosh said:
In other words, the British government paid to the Dominion of Canada $182 million in excess of the price quoted in the contract.
To me this was rather shocking. I came to the conclusion that one cannot take too seriously everything that is said in the House of Commons.
Last night the hon. member for Timis-kaming made a great speech on the feed mills. He went on at great length to say that wheat was selling now at 50 cents less than the price at which it should be selling. He said that the farmers producing beef in western Canada got the advantage of this 50 cents. He mentioned this 50 cents time and time again, and I pretty nearly reached out and caught it. Where he got it from I am still in doubt. His whole speech reminded me of the speech he made in the House of Commons a year ago on wheat board permits. The committee will remember that last year we discussed wheat board permits and the whole quota system for quite some time. I listened to the hon. member for Timiskam-ing for quite a while at that time. I spoke to him afterwards and I said, "Surely you did not grasp how the quota system works".
I went on at great length to explain it to him. He said, "Oh, I see how it works now but still, it does not matter; I had to fill in the time, anyway". I gathered from the remarks he made in his speech last evening-

It aggravated me to some extent to hear the hon. member for Timiskaming say that the feed mill regulations would put western farmers in a better position than eastern farmers with regard to feeding livestock. I could not understand this. As I mentioned earlier, he went on to talk about a figure of 50 cents and he referred to 50 cents so many times that one could almost visualize that 50-cent piece. Actually, however, under the feed mill regulations western farmers will be able to buy western grain no more cheaply than they have been able to buy it in the past. In fact, allowing the feed mills to come into the picture and handle feed grain will have a tendency to increase the price farmers are paying for feed grain because it will create a greater market for such grain. If anything, it will have a tendency to increase the price of feed grains sold to farmers.
Farmers who are feeding cattle in western Canada now will be in the same position as that in which they were in the past or perhaps will not be quite as well off from a financial point of view. They may be able to get a better concentration of feeds or a better mixing of feeds. I hope that will be so, but certainly there is no 50-cent piece in evidence as the hon. member for Timiskaming tried to indicate last night. This is borne out by the figures the Minister of Agriculture put on Hansard indicating what feed mills are paying for coarse grains. He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is twofold, first, to encourage the development of industry in the four Atlantic provinces and, second, to reduce the high level of unemployment in those areas where it persists. It has been my view that the Industrial Development Bank Act, which legislation has been made available to assist in the establishment of industries in Canada, has not had in the Atlantic area that beneficial effect that one would have expected from this legislation when it was placed on the statute books. It may be that statistics will emphasize the situation more forcibly to all members of the house.
In the six years from 1955 to 1960 inclusive the following numbers of loans through the industrial development bank were made available to industries in the Atlantic provinces:	Newfoundland, 21; Prince Edward
Island, 19; Nova Scotia, 114; and New Brunswick, 116 loans, or a total of 270 loans during this period. For the sake of comparison I point out that in the same period in the province of Ontario 937 loans were made available to industry and in the year 1960, 264 loans were made, only six less than were made available to the four Atlantic provinces in six years.
From a monetary standpoint the imbalance of this situation is still more significant, with the four Atlantic provinces receiving less than one tenth of the over-all amount lent to the 10 provinces, a matter of slightly more than $18 million compared with $192 million, or a percentage figure of less than 10 per cent.
When one compares the situation in existence here with the repeated comments of experts, that the prime need of the Atlantic

Private Bills
provinces is cheap investment capital which must of necessity come from outside our area because of the low level of the earning power in the maritimes-37 per cent on a per capita basis below the average for residents of the central or western provinces-one quickly realizes the need for bold and imaginative steps to rectify the situation. In recent times the Atlantic provinces have shown a very real interest in their own problems and have taken many steps on their own to remedy the situation wherever this is financially possible.
An example of this action in my province of Nova Scotia was the establishment by the Stanfield government of a crown corporation known as "Industrial Estates Limited". Another example was the appointment of A. K. Cairncross, an eminent British economist, to study and report on the economic situation in the Atlantic area. This report was made available to the provincial government in February of this year, and the conclusions reached by this economist will no doubt be of lasting benefit in correcting the situation wherever the provinces find this possible within their limited resources.
In this report Professor Cairncross indicates a number of methods whereby the federal government could assist our area in attracting new and expanding established industries.
As all members are aware, in the supplementary budget, this government took the first step that has ever been taken by any federal government in its efforts to assist areas with persistent unemployment in attracting new industries, through the principle of double depreciation. Some have said since this step was taken that the government has not gone far enough. Very recently Conservatives from across this country, in convention, passed a resolution requesting that tax incentives for new and expanding industry in our coal mining areas be provided on a scale more generous than presently proposed.
In recent days Mr. Frank Sobey, president of the Nova Scotia crown company, Industrial Estates Limited, when appearing before that legislature's industry committee, stated that this crown corporation could attract industries into depressed areas of Nova Scotia if it had additional help from the federal government enabling the crown corporation to offer tax concessions or start-up concessions, or other types of concessions of this nature that would make Nova Scotia locations attractive. The bill that I have before the house at the present time would do exactly what the president of Industrial Estates requests.
Its basic premise is the co-operation of the directors of the industrial development bank with the industrial estate corporations in the

Atlantic provinces. It would allow the industrial development bank to lend moneys to industrial estate companies to assist in providing premises for industrial enterprises. Further, it would allow the bank to make to such companies annual grants which could be used to make payments of interest on the moneys borrowed until such time as the said company or companies were in a financial position to do so from their earnings.
Further, in areas of persistent high level unemployment it would allow the bank, working in co-operation with the industrial estate companies, to go even further and consider ways and means of providing still further incentives to convince these investors they should locate in these areas. In this regard may I bring to the attention of members of this house an editorial recently published in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald which comments on Professor A. K. Cairncross' report which emphasizes a situation that is not usually given the consideration it merits. The article appeared on March 1, 1961, under the heading "An Epidemic Force" and reads as follows:
One particular piece of basic philosophy to be found in the report on the ills of the Atlantic provinces which has just been submitted by Professor A. K. Cairncross of Glasgow university should be necessary reading and re-reading for all those in governmental positions of responsibility for tackling ihis growing problem. It is this:-
The article then quotes from the report as follows:
"The mere existence of a chronic labour surplus is usually sufficient to generate obstacles to development in the habits and outlook of the population. The pace of work becomes slowed down where unemployment is a frequent recurrence. Why hurry towards idleness or work under pressure where others could lend a hand? Ambition is curbed, the response to economic incentives is blunted, mobility is reduced and hopes of a higher standard of living are stifled. Thus even the opportunities that plainly exist may be neglected and the failure of the community may be attributed to apathy, laziness or lack of enterprise."
This is the third year that I have placed this bill before the house, but I feel certain there never has been a time when its debate has been more appropriate than now. Very recently in my constituency of Cumberland the very fine citizens of Joggins were informed that the coal mine upon which the area depends for a livelihood is to be closed forthwith. This situation coupled with the one that has been in existence in the disaster scarred town of Springhill, indicates that new, realistic, bold, imaginative and immediate steps must be taken if they are to have the opportunity to secure new types of industry to employ the responsible, willing and able working force available to them.
The submission that I make which is included in this bill is not an unrealistic one

but one that has been tried and proven successful in Italy, Belgium and France, and in those areas of England, Scotland and Wales, where unemployment was persistent. It has been proven in Puerto Rico and now has been adopted in the United States. I see no reason why we cannot, and should not, go forward immediately and give to the Atlantic area that hope, which they must have and certainly deserve and which is inherent in this bill.
I know my constituency is not the only one in the Atlantic provinces that suffers from this dilemma at the present time. I am quite certain that it is not necessary for me to point out the problems of these other areas, for they have seated in this house able and energetic representatives who I am certain will be only too anxious to express their own opinion, if the time is available to them, under this particular bill.

Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to give my wholehearted support to the bill which has just been introduced by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates), an act to provide for the development of certain provinces by distribution of industries and by reduction of unemployment therein.
There is no need for me to repeat my view regarding this particular matter so far as the Atlantic provinces are concerned. I have spoken in this house on many occasions, and have brought forward the needs of the Atlantic provinces. Speaking on the last supply motion on Monday of this week I expressed the policy of the official opposition with regard to the development of the Atlantic provinces. I mentioned at the time that the double depreciation measure for depressed areas introduced by the government was insufficient and would not provide the remedy which is required to take care of the situation.
The situation in the Atlantic provinces at this time is certainly not the best. The latest unemployment figures which were released on Tuesday of this week show that in the middle of February we had 101,000 unemployed people in the Atlantic provinces. This figure represents an increase of 17,000 over and above the figures which were released for the month of January this year. This means that out of a total increase in unemployment of 26,000 persons for the whole of the country, 17,000 or 65 per cent of that increase came from the Atlantic provinces. It is no wonder that we on this side of the house are concerned about this problem, and we are pleased that for a change one of the government members agrees with us and 90205-6-211
Private Bills
admits that we need special measures and special incentives, to take care of this situation.
The bill introduced by the hon. member is in line with the policy which has been expressed by the official opposition. It is in line with the resolutions which were discussed at the Liberal rally held early in January.
I know that effective measures must be taken at once to take care of the situation, particularly in the Cape Breton area where coal mines will be closing almost regularly starting from the month of May and continuing for the balance of this year.
It is most unfortunate that the present government has not realized the seriousness of the situation before this time, when it is too late. The government should have realized the seriousness of the situation in 1958 when we of the official opposition disclosed the situation as we then saw it and as we felt it would become in the years to follow. As I have said, the action taken by the government has been insufficient and has not taken care of this situation. If the government are prepared to accept the provisions which are included in this bill, we are sure they would at least alleviate the situation.
It is most unfortunate that an area like the Atlantic provinces, with natural resources at their disposal, is being deprived of secondary industry and does not receive the share of industry which it deserves in order to maintain its economy in the same manner as the rest of Canada.
Under the present administration individual workers in rural areas-tradesmen such as carpenters and so on-who have been receiving unemployment insurance benefits in years past have this year been deprived of those benefits. A few moments ago I received a letter from an individual in my constituency who employed a carpenter last summer for a period of four and a half months. That man was disqualified from receiving unemployment insurance benefits-

On a point of order, Mr Speaker, this is a very important bill which members from the maritimes would like to discuss. I think the hon. member for Gloucester should be confined to the point before the house and should not waste the short time which we have to discuss this very important matter.

Mr. Speaker, the bill now before us reads:
An act to provide for the development of certain provinces by the distribution of industry and for the reduction of unemployment therein.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the point of order is well taken. The application of the Unemployment Insurance Act has really nothing to do with this bill, the purpose of

Private Bills
which is related to the Atlantic provinces, whereas the Unemployment Insurance Act applies to the whole of the country.

I will abide by your ruling, Mr. Speaker. Nevertheless I wish to repeat that the measures introduced so far, such as the double depreciation measure which was included in the baby budget, do not meet the needs of the Atlantic provinces. In the Atlantic provinces we need additional capital and tax incentives. This situation will not be remedied by allowing new industry double depreciation for one year. That measure will not improve the situation.
I wish to repeat what I said earlier. I completely support this bill. I agree with the hon. member for Cumberland, and I hope that this time all hon. members from the Atlantic provinces, whatever their political affiliations, will be in agreement and will support the measure.

Mr. Speaker, I should first of all like to extend my heartiest congratulations to the dynamic hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) who has brought this very important bill before the house this afternoon. I think my greatest pleasure while serving in the House of Commons to date has been in my association with other hon. members from my province and indeed from the whole Atlantic area. These hon. members have always endeavoured to keep the problems of the Atlantic region before the government. One of the foremost leaders at all times in this effort has been the hon. member for Cumberland.
It is important to note that Bill No. C-23 introduced by the hon. member for Cumberland pinpoints one of the chief problems of the Atlantic area. Our chief problem is to develop further manufacturing industry in the area which will provide more employment. Indeed, I could not help but remark to myself, while the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) was speaking, how little had been done in all the years when the party of which he is a member was the government of this country. I also remarked how much the unemployment problem which we have in the Atlantic provinces today is due to the carelessness of that administration and the fact that in those days there were so few people to speak out for the Atlantic area.
It is particularly apt that this bill should come before the house at this time, when we are experiencing such great difficulty in the coal industry in Cape Breton. This is a difficulty which has been advancing over the years. It is paramount at this time because of the surplus fuel oil, residual oil, hydro power and natural gas upon the Montreal market

in particular. It is too bad that in the days when the hon. member for Gloucester was on the government side of the house he did not bring to the attention of the government of that day the effect upon the coal industry of the maritimes, of the completion of the natural gas pipe line to Montreal.
Indeed, one of the reasons for the problem we have today in the coal industry is the surplus gas being pumped to our traditional markets in Montreal and east. It is a shame that this fact was not brought to the attention of the former government which sponsored that pipe line prior to 1957.
Many of our industries in the Atlantic provinces are doing very well at the moment. Our tourist industry has grown very appreciably in the last few years. Much of the credit for that growth is due to the considerable expansion in our national parks and in the development of other tourist activities in our region. Much of it is due also to the new roads which have been constructed through the greatly increased grants made available to the Atlantic area since 1957.
As I am sure the hon. member for Gloucester will agree, the fishing industry is growing steadily in all Atlantic areas, and we look forward to an expanding market and to an increased sale of fish products in the years ahead. Our dragger fleets are growing, our fish plants are generally busier than in previous years and we can expect this resource industry of the Atlantic area to continue to expand. In Nova Scotia in particular there has also been a great increase in the market for pulpwood over recent years. At the moment I am proud to say that in my own riding at Point Tupper there is being built at a cost of about $40 million, a pulp mill which will almost double the demand for pulpwood in the province. In addition, there is an increased demand for pulp for export. Generally speaking, while we must grapple with the problems of our declining coal industry, we rejoice in the fact that a new door is opening and that the forest industries will provide increased employment.
Agriculture, too, stimulated by the new market for pulp, which means extra cash in the hands of the farmers, is increasing in importance. Certainly our problem is not one of surpluses but rather one of production. The effort being made in all the Atlantic provinces, but particularly in my province, to increase agricultural production is one of which we can all be proud and one which augurs well for the general economic future of the region.
However, I should like to point out that resource industries, such as fishing, agriculture and forestry are activities of a type

which do not effectively remove seasonal unemployment. This has been the case for many years and the situation can be cured only by an industrialization program of some kind which would mean more employment of that type in the Atlantic area. Some big strides have been made toward increasing manufacturing production in the Atlantic provinces. As the hon. member for Cumberland has mentioned, Industrial Estates, with the encouragement of the Stanfield government in Nova Scotia, has fostered the establishment of a substantial number of new industries and, the new mill at Point Tupper, about which I spoke a moment ago, is the first major manufacturing plant to be established in Nova Scotia since the Mersey pulp mill was established in 1925. In all these years between 1925 and 1960 no substantial new large industry was established in the province. It has been owing to the forwardlooking confidence and faith of the premier of Nova Scotia and the dynamism of his government that there has been a stimulation of industrial manufacturing and industrial settlement in the province and we all hope very much that this process will continue.
I spoke a moment ago of a number of our resource industries which are now doing very well, though we lack sufficient manufacturing plants. I might say also that the primary steel plant in Sydney which supplies much of the steel sold in Canada had a good year in 1960. It enlarged its markets. It is very efficient and it is able to compete with most other primary producers on this continent. The men who are employed in this industry are grateful in particular to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) for his help to the company when it was seeking out new orders in 1960.
However, the general problem of establishing industries in the Atlantic area has not been solved. What strides we are making, and I do not minimize them, have been against the tide that runs against the Atlantic provinces owing to our geographical position. We are a long distance from the markets which our manufactured goods must find in Ontario and Quebec. Manufacturing industries in the Atlantic provinces which sell goods in the central provinces are at a disadvantage. They have to bear the extra cost of maintaining a sales force far from home, and the lack of a large local market to help set up the primary source of sales which is so important particularly to infant industries.
An example of the difficulties under which industry labours in the Atlantic area is to be found in the experience we have encountered in trying to coax into Nova Scotia 90205-6-2 lli
Private Bills
the new rolling mill, which Dosco proposes to build on the St. Lawrence river east of Montreal. One of the most important markets for primary steel is that provided by the demand for cold rolled products. If Dosco's primary steel mill at Sydney is to enjoy stable markets in the future it is very important that the corporation build a cold rolling mill to process Sydney ingots. We from Nova Scotia have been pressing for the construction of the mill in Cape Breton Island. A new industry such as this would give a tremendous uplift to our economy.
However, Dosco insists that, to be economically successful, the mill must be located close to its potential market which would be in the Montreal area. It says that it is only one of several firms considering locating in Quebec and that if it does not move into the area, some other steel company will do so. Their position is that it would be of no advantage to Nova Scotia to have a cold rolling mill built in the province if in a few years Stelco or some other processor moved into Quebec, where it would be in a position to capture a large portion of the Quebec market. They also say that transportation difficulties are not the only problem since, while transportation subsidies might equalize prices for a company manufacturing in Nova Scotia, the company in Quebec, as a local industry with its headquarters in the area, would have a distinct selling advantage and be able to offer better delivery service and more convenient contact for custom and special work.
If there is any way in which these difficulties can be overcome, the construction of the proposed rolling mill in Cape Breton would go a long way towards solving our present coal industry crisis. But if the mill must, for economic factors beyond control be built at Contrecoeur or some site along the St. Lawrence, then it is vital that special transportation assistance be provided to carry primary steel from Sydney to the rolling plant, wherever it may be built.
The Atlantic provinces in general have been very pleased with the special help which has been provided since 1957. The Atlantic adjustment grants are in themselves an example of this. Over-all grants to the Atlantic provinces, conditional and unconditional, have doubled since 1957. Moreover, other provisions of this government, although not specifically designed for the Atlantic area, will be of great benefit to my province. I refer to such projects as the vocational training program. Only the other day the premier of Nova Scotia announced the building of a vocational training school on Cape Breton Island. It is a school in connection with which

Private Bills
there will be no need for assistance from the municipalities. This will be of great help in training men in the eastern part of Nova Scotia. However, in order to strike at the root of the problem of seasonal unemployment in Nova Scotia we need more than anything else to develop more manufacturing industry. Only manufacturing can provide us with the steady year-round employment which we need in order to give stability to our economy.
We can have manufacturing industry if in some way we are able to equalize the profits that an entrepreneur can earn in Nova Scotia, or any other province in the Atlantic area, and those available to him in the other provinces. Regardless of transportation subsidies which we must have and regardless of other aid which may be made available to the Atlantic area, unless we can provide as great a profit to a manufacturer in the Atlantic area as he can find in the more populous areas of Canada then we will have a difficult time in establishing industry there.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Cumberland we need special assistance to help us in the financing of industries in the Atlantic area. It is not as easy to provide financing for manufacturing there as it is in other areas. We should like to have that special help in a manner suggested in the bill presented by the hon. member for Cumberland. We also need tax concessions to help us equalize profit opportunities in the area. Because of transportation and other difficulties it is not possible to earn the same ratio of profit. Therefore it does not seem fair to me that a company in the Atlantic area faced with all the obstacles involved in manufacturing there should have to pay as high a corporation tax as do manufacturing companies elsewhere in Canada. If we could say to the owner of a company that might locate in the Atlantic area that even though his profits might be lower, he would have a lower rate of corporation income tax to pay over the period he would be in the area, I am sure this inducement would mean the difference between his company locating in our area as against a more populous or more geographically-favoured region of the country.
I feel it is only through the establishment of industry in that area with the help of transportation subsidies and the availability of industrial credit and above all of tax concessions to equalize profit opportunities that we can overcome the far-reaching problems of the Atlantic area in relation to the attraction and development of manufacturing industry.
As I have said, we from the province of Nova Scotia and from other parts of the

Atlantic area are grateful for the consideration that has been given to our problems by the government to date. It is certainly quite a change from the attitude that existed in the period of which I spoke from 1925 to 1955 when so little progress was made in terms of providing new employment sources or potential in the Atlantic area. However, I suggest to the government that in taking further steps to help us become self-sufficient, and to help us earn our way in this great and expanding nation, nothing is more important than to encourage the development of manufacturing industry to provide employment in Nova Scotia and the Atlantic area. At this particular time when we in Nova Scotia are faced with the dire threat of mine closures it is more important now than at any other time that the government give all possible consideration to such concessions as will induce manufacturing industry to settle in the Atlantic area.

Mr. Speaker, while this bill is addressed to a particular section of the country from which I, like so many other hon. members of this house, do not come, all our interests are so interdependent that there could be nothing but encouragement for participation in this debate by hon. members who come from sections of Canada other than the maritime provinces.
I rise to speak in support of the principle and indeed much of the content of this bill because if there is any section of our country that needs the kind of assistance envisaged in this bill, it is the Atlantic provinces area. I refer to the four Atlantic provinces and particularly, perhaps, those on the mainland. I well recall the speech made in this house on Monday last by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) who outlined the economic conditions prevailing in the maritime provinces and indeed the remedies which he proposed encompassed many of the provisions of this bill. The discussion we had on that occasion had to do with a matter which in principle involved the recommendations contained in the operative parts of this bill.
We have heard from the hon. member who has just taken his seat and from various other hon. members who participated in the discussion on the previous occasion and from the hon. member for Gloucester today about the background of economic and social conditions in the maritimes at the present time which warrant our support of this measure. These matters should serve as notice to the government of not only the desirability but the vital urgency for the government to take measures more formidable than those now before us, not only to correct the situation in that section of the country but to deal with similar

conditions that prevail to a greater or lesser degree in every part of our nation.
The facts of the situation in the Atlantic provinces are these. Eighteen per cent of the labour force in the Atlantic provinces is out of work, according to the latest figures given to this house officially on Wednesday last.

May I ask
the hon. gentleman a question? Does that figure not incude a high percentage of fishermen?

In reply to my hon. friend let me say first of all that fishermen are not included in the figures. That was as a result of a decision taken by this government two years ago. In addition to that whether or not they are included, I do not know why my hon. friend in particular should regard fishermen as being less deserving of remedial legislation in the matter of unemployment than any other segment of the working force.
I do not.

The point is that on the basis of the last available figures 18 per cent of the working force in the maritime area is out of work. That percentage is so much greater than the national average of 11.3 per cent as to give any hon. member of this house cause to be greatly concerned about conditions in the Atlantic provinces. There was an increase in the last reported figure of some 23,000 more Canadians out of work than in the previous reported period and of that 23,000 no less than 17,000 come from the Atlantic area. Those are alarming facts.
It seems to me this bill, which I should like to see receive immediate passage, is one which if implemented by the government would not immediately but would in the foreseeable future provide the kind of encouragement for the relocation of industry that might materially assist the maritime provinces. The immediate problem in the Atlantic area, however, is not covered by this bill. The immediate problem is that 2,800 miners will be out of work as a result of the shutdown of mines at the end of May. That is a matter of grave concern to everybody in the maritime provinces and particularly to people in places like Glace Bay, Sydney Mines and Waterford. It is a matter of serious concern to all people of Canada that at the end of May the mines will be shut down and at least 2,800 miners will be out of work in adition to those miners who are already unemployed.
When we realize the problem in regard to the relationship between the lack of certain
Private Bills
skills and the availability of employment, we can well appreciate what this is going to mean in human terms to so many people in the Atlantic provinces and indirectly, on that account, to Canada as a whole. While this bill is commendable and touches upon the type of thing we have been advocating in our criticism of the government's program of double depreciation designed to assist areas of chronic unemployment, I should hasten to say this. The measure now before us will not solve the immediate problem that confronts the coal miners in the Atlantic provinces and in particular in the areas I have mentioned.
Of course, this bill is worthy of support because it highlights the weakness of the program announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in his baby budget speech on December 20. In his only reference to unemployment the minister said that the government was going to try to meet the national emergency by a system of accelerated depreciation, particularly described as double depreciation, in order to assist industries in relocating and to encourage industries already established in areas of chronic unemployment to stay there. We have criticized the government's program of double depreciation because of its limited extent. A program of double depreciation that is to be in force for only one year is, of course, of no great consequence. I have made the statement-and it has not been challenged by the Minister of Finance-that the program will not bring one industry to one community in Canada. That being so-and it is supported by the evidence of those who have no political interest in making comments on the government's depreciation program-it reveals that the government is lacking in its approach to the whole problem of unemployment.
If the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) would come forward with a bill or an announcement based upon section 11 of the Income Tax Act, which would incorporate some of the provision, in this bill, we would not have the same substantial grounds for criticism of that measure as we have had, because in this bill the hon. member proposes a form of accelerated depreciation, but he also proposes loans to assist enterprises in reducing high unemployment. He proposes that there should be bank grants to acceptable persons or companies to be used in the establishment of or assistance to industrial enterprises. Bank loans and development loans are the things that are now being tackled and are part of

the crash program being undertaken in the United States in its program of accelerated depreciation.
This bill is valuable not only for what it proposes but for what it exposes, namely the weaknesses in the government's declared policy to meet the situation not only in the maritime provinces but throughout Canada generally. I could go on commending this bill, pointing out its good features and comparing them with the weaknesses and the wants of the government's own program; but so anxious am I, as are other hon. members in this party, to see this bill pass so that it can be used as a sanction on the government to take a more vigorous step to do something about this serious problem of unemployment that now obtains in the maritime provinces that I will not do so. These figures cannot be scoffed at; they cannot be ignored. When 18 per cent of the working force of the maritime provinces is out of work it is a matter of the gravest concern not only to that area but to everyone in this house. The government of the day, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) and other ministers in the house today, along with the minister without portfolio from Newfoundland should rise in their places-
Mr. Speaker, may I draw to the hon. gentleman's attention that I have been promoted to the office of Solicitor General?
I did the minister a great injustice.
What about the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) ?
I wish the Minister of National Health and Welfare had been here when we were discussing old age pensions earlier this afternoon.
He was here.

here. I invited him to take part in the debate. I want to say to the hon. member I regret I referred to him as the minister without portfolio. Of course, I knew he was Solicitor General. It was only because one is tired at the end of a long week that one makes these errors. I wish to say that the hon. gentleman deserves a much more effective and important post than that of Solicitor General. I would have hoped that the government would recognize the maritime provinces by using not only the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) from that area but also the productive capacities of the Solicitor General who could add to his general legal knowledge, his knowledge of the maritimes and of Newfoundland and push this slow-moving government into action. speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the mover of this bill, but we should like to draw to the attention of the hon. member the fact that this bill should apply not only to the four maritime provinces but to all of Canada. The need is as great in a number of other mining areas as it is in the maritimes. I presume the maritimes are generous enough to give us the opportunity of receiving the benefits that they and other parts of Canada also need very badly.
I hope we shall have the opportunity of amending this bill when the appropriate time comes.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to talk out this bill because it is a very important one. I see the time is getting short, but I do want to indicate my support of this measure and to make one or two observations with regard to my own province. There is nothing in this bill that has not been proposed on many occasions in the past. If we are to put this bill into effect we must realize that, however desirable it is to attract industry to the maritime provinces, the economic laws cannot be completely ignored. In my opinion, a rational program will first of all utilize the resources that are available in any particular area. In my own province, of course, the main industry is fishing and I think a great deal could be done to modernize this industry, to improve marketing and to reduce the cost of operations.
As far as manufacturing industries are concerned, of necessity they must be on a small scale. There again, they should utilize the skills and materials that are available there. I should like to recall to the house that in the early days the great industry in the maritimes was shipbuilding. We have a great tradition in the building of ships, and great skills not only in building them but in managing them and sailing them. A great deal of our prosperity in days gone by was based on that fact alone. We need a shipbuilding industry in Canada, and I think that is one thing that should be given much more encouragement than is the case at present. It is all right to concentrate the shipbuilding industry in one or two places but this is something that the maritime provinces can

do as well as or even better than other parts of Canada. I should like to see a special shipbuilding program introduced particularly for the benefit of the maritime provinces.
I am going to take only another minute to say that whatever are the industries we establish in the maritime provinces and in my own province in particular, they will not survive unless something is done about transportation because over the years every industry that we have managed to get started has foundered on transportation costs. 1 am speaking from memory but I do not believe that the bill makes provision for any special concessions for industries in the maritimes with regard to freight rates. That is an absolute "must" if we are going to do anything of a concrete nature.
I think it is shortsightedness on the part of big business in other parts of Canada not to realize that a nation cannot exist, as our deputy minister of economic development said a short while ago, half rich and half poor. It is in the interests of the richer provinces to spend some of their money in developing industries in those provinces which are not so well off, thus raising the standards in those provinces. In my own little province of Newfoundland we already constitute a market with a value of some $250 million for the central provinces. This could be expanded to a billion dollar market if industries were developed in our province even to a small extent. I do not want to take any more time. I hope that the government will take the bill seriously and that it will be given swift passage through the house.

subsubtopic: PAVING, PARENT, QUE.
speechtext:
1. In 1959, did the Department of National Defence contribute in any way to the cost of paving approximately one mile of the main road through the village of Parent, Laviolette county, Quebec, including the raising of several manholes of existing sewers?
2.	If so: (a) for what reason? (b) what was the cost involved to the Department of National Defence? (c) who was responsible for the work carried out in regard to (i) planning (ii) supervision (iii) actually doing the work? (d) in the event that the Department of National Defence was responsible for any item under (c), why was the department thus responsible?
Answer by: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of
National Defence):
1.	Yes.
2.	(a) To improve the road access to R.C.A.F. station Parent.
(b)	$42,792.92 with the village of Parent committed by an agreement, dated June 17, 1958, to contribute 25 per cent of this amount.
(c)	(i) Department of National Defence.
(ii)	Defence Construction Limited.
(iii)	Paquin Construction Company, Val D'Or, P.Q.

maintopic: AUTOMATIC CROSSING PROTECTION, EDINBURGH DRIVE, MONCTON
AUTOMATIC CROSSING PROTECTION, EDINBURGH DRIVE, MONCTON
speechtext:
1. Did the board of transport commissioners for Canada receive an application from the Department of Public Works of the province of New Brunswick for the installation of automatic protection of the railway level crossing at Edinburgh drive in the greater Moncton area?
Questions
2.	If so, when was the request received, and what is the present status of the same?
3.	If a grade separation was requested instead of automatic protection, to what extent would the board authorize a grant from the railway grade crossing fund, and how would the balance of the cost be apportioned, including future maintenance?
Answer by: Hon. Leon Balcer (Minister of
Transport):
The board of transport commissioners for Canada advise as follows:
1.	Yes.
2.	The New Brunswick department of public works submitted a letter to the board dated February 3, 1961 requesting that automatic protection be installed at the level crossing across the Canadian National Railways at Edinburgh drive in greater Moncton area and by letter dated February 23, 1961 withdrew its request for protection at this crossing, advising that the department proposes to make an application for a grade separation at this location.
3.	The board may authorize a grant from the railway grade crossing fund to the extent of 80 per cent of the cost of constructing a grade separation which will eliminate an existing level crossing which has been in existence for at least three years not to exceed, however, the sum of $500,000. If the total cost of constructing a grade separation does not exceed $625,000 and if a grant is authorized from the railway grade crossing fund to the extent of 80 per cent of the cost of construction, the railway company is required to pay 5 per cent and the highway authority having jurisdiction over the highway is required to pay 15 per cent, all in accordance with section 9 of the board's general order 848. If the total cost of a grade separation is in excess of $625,000, the board may authorize a grant from the railway grade crossing fund, not to exceed $500,000, with the balance of the cost to be borne and paid by the railway company and the highway authority in accordance with agreement reached between the railway company and the highway authority, or as the board may direct. The cost of future maintenance of such grade separation would be borne by the highway authority in the case of an overhead bridge and by the railway company in the case of a subway.
